title: Prompt with Purpose
summary: After completing this intermediate module, a learner can turn a vague request into a purposeful prompt with a defined outcome, relevant context, constraints, and success criteria. The learner can also test and revise that prompt systematically.
objectives: Define the intended outcome of a prompt before writing its instructions.
Write a prompt that includes relevant context, explicit constraints, and a requested output structure.
Create success criteria that make a response easier to evaluate.
Test a prompt, identify one specific weakness, and revise one element at a time.

sections.title: Intermediate level and learning outcome
paragraphs: This is an intermediate module. It assumes that you can already write a basic natural-language instruction and read a generated response. It does not assume specialized programming, research, or statistical knowledge.

Before this module, you may be able to ask for an output without defining how to judge it. Afterwards, you can design a prompt around a specific purpose, state what an acceptable response must contain, and revise the prompt using evidence from a test response.

sections.title: Define the purpose first
paragraphs: A purposeful prompt begins with an intended outcome rather than an opening sentence. Ask what the response will help someone decide, create, understand, or verify. Replace a broad aim such as explain this topic with an observable outcome such as produce a comparison that helps a reader choose between two approaches.

Next, define success criteria. These are properties you can inspect in the response, such as whether it addresses the named audience, covers required points, respects a length limit, or uses the requested structure. A criterion should be specific enough that you can decide whether the response met it.

The cited paper presents prompt construction as a form of programming through natural language. In this module, that perspective means treating the prompt as a designed set of instructions that can be tested and revised rather than as a single improvised question.
sections.callout: Write the intended outcome and success criteria before drafting the full prompt.

sections.title: Assemble the prompt
paragraphs: Start with the task. State the action the response should perform, such as compare, classify, explain, extract, or revise. Name the intended audience when its knowledge or needs should influence the response.

Add only the context needed to complete the task. Relevant context can include definitions, background facts, source material, or the decision the response will support. Separating supplied facts from requested instructions helps a reader identify what information the response should use.

State constraints explicitly. A constraint can limit scope, length, tone, permitted evidence, or required coverage. Avoid relying on vague quality words alone. For example, concise is open to interpretation, while use no more than three paragraphs provides a checkable boundary.

Describe the output structure when structure matters. You might request a short comparison followed by a recommendation, or a table with named columns. Finish by stating the success criteria that will be used to review the response.

sections.title: Turn a vague request into a purposeful prompt
paragraphs: Consider the vague request: Explain data retention. Its purpose, audience, scope, and acceptable output are unclear.

A purposeful version is: Explain data retention to staff who handle customer records but do not set policy. Define the term, describe two reasons an organization may retain records, distinguish retention from permanent storage, and identify two questions staff should ask before keeping a record. Use no more than four short paragraphs and do not invent a retention period.

The revised prompt states a task, audience, required coverage, output limit, and boundary against unsupported detail. Its requirements also provide success criteria: a reviewer can check for the definition, two reasons, the distinction, two questions, the paragraph limit, and the absence of an invented period.

sections.title: Test and revise systematically
paragraphs: Run the prompt with a representative input, then compare the response with each success criterion. Record a specific mismatch rather than judging the response only as good or bad. A useful diagnosis might be that the response omitted the audience's decision, exceeded the requested length, or treated a required distinction as optional.

Revise one prompt element that plausibly caused the mismatch. If the output omitted a required distinction, make that distinction an explicit requirement. If the structure varied too much, name the required sections. Changing one element at a time makes it easier to connect a revision with its effect.

Retest with the original input and at least one different but representative input. A prompt is ready for its intended use when its responses repeatedly satisfy the stated criteria across those tests. If the criteria themselves prove unclear or irrelevant, revise the purpose and criteria before adjusting wording again.

questions.prompt: What should be defined before drafting the full prompt?
choices: The intended outcome and success criteria
questions.explanation: The module instructs learners to define the intended outcome and checkable success criteria before drafting the full prompt.

questions.prompt: Which instruction is the clearest checkable constraint?
choices: Use no more than three paragraphs
questions.explanation: A limit of three paragraphs can be checked directly. The other choices depend on subjective interpretations that the prompt does not define.

questions.prompt: After a test response omits a required distinction, what revision process does the module recommend?
choices: Change several unrelated requirements at once
Make the distinction explicit, change one element, and retest
Accept the response without comparing it with the criteria
questions.explanation: The module recommends diagnosing a specific mismatch, revising the relevant prompt element, and retesting so the effect of the change can be observed.
